utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I understand there is a matter counsel wish to raise. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, good afternoon to all. Thank you very much. In actual fact, what the Defence teams want to do is answer the issues raised by my learned friend, Mr. Moore, on Friday, during our last session on Friday, in relation to two specific matters. One is an answer to your question about agreed facts and facts that are still in dispute. The other issue is about the dead-lines for any documentation concerning witness interviews conducted by either party. As for agreed facts and facts still in dispute, what I wish to say, Your Honour, is that we have held a number of informal meetings with our learned friends from the OTP. The result was the fact that I informed you about back in January. We succeeded in agreeing on 34 points. That agreement was reached in January this year. We also confirmed our agreement to our learned friends at OTP in writing, upon which Mr. Moore sent us a request in addition -- in relation to another fact concerning the location of the Grabovo exhumation site. We informed the OTP that as far as the facts concerning Grabovo were concerned, we had already agreed to two substantial theories that we were able to. But the way the Prosecution framed a possible agreement concerning the fact was unacceptable to the Defence because it is even outside the scope of the indictment itself. As for the location itself, that of Grabovo, the Defence agreed when the location was first found that everything was done in a professional and impeccable manner. We did not challenge the identities of certain persons found there whose bodies were autopsied and identified in accordance with the rules and standards governing DNA analysis. I believe that even as early as late January the situation was ripe for all this information to be submitted to the Trial Chamber. I believe we, the Defence teams, have done our best to make progress. We are still willing to continue our conversation was our friends from the OTP throughout this trial concerning any facts that emerge, and we shall make an effort to agree on as many facts as possible. I do believe, however, that most of the agreed facts can now be submitted to the Trial Chamber because as a matter of fact these facts have been agreed. There may be additional matters in the course of this trial resulting from our future conversations, and these matters may in turn result in an additional agreement. As for the other matter concerning dead-lines, my learned friend, Mr. Moore, put forward his proposal that both parties should submit any documents to be used in examination within 24 to 48 hours. What you said, Your Honours, about the substance of what cross-examination really means and the objective of any cross-examination as part of a defence, if one agrees to have the fundamental orthodox rule changed that the Defence has no obligation to serve any documents on the OTP, but rather that the OTP is the only party to have this obligation to serve documents upon the Defence, I think the practice that has been used so far, the 24-hour dead-line, will be quite sufficient in view of the fact that the objective is, at least in my understanding, the objective of having this dead-line at all, is to leave the parties sufficient time to possibly challenge the authenticity of certain documents. I believe that to be the essence of this dead-line issue and also in order to have sufficient time to prepare our cross-examination. The established practice so far during this trial, I believe, has shown that no major problems occurred about this, and the trial went as smoothly as we all hoped it would. It is for this reason that I still believe that the 48-hour dead-line proposed by my learned friend, Mr. Moore, to be too long, and I believe such a long dead-line would affect the effectiveness of our cross-examination, especially in the light of the fact that the Defence happens to be in a position concerning some aspects of our cross-examination in such a position that we depend on what the witness may or may not say during certain stages of examination-in-chief. Bearing this in mind, a 48-hour dead-line would be impossible to deal with, since as we all know, the Defence only gets to cross-examine a witness once the OTP has finished. Furthermore, the Defence believes that all 65 ter documents should be exempt from this rule, all such documents as have been [Realtime transcript read in error "Vujic being"] served on us by our friends from the OTP. These are documents that they are familiar with and with which they find no fault. This also happens to be the main purpose or objective for setting any dead-lines at all. As for the Rule 68 documents that have been served on us, the same applies as set out in my previous conclusion. These documents were known to my learned friends in good time. They served the documents on us, and they had sufficient time to check the authenticity of any documents included in that set. Your Honours, that is all I have to say about these two issues. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Vasic. Mr. Lukic, I was about to ask whether Mr. Borovic wanted to add anything. I will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. I just wish to keep up good relations with the Trial Chamber and keep my own position from perhaps becoming a little too aggressive as was the case the last time around. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: A new week, Mr. Borovic, yes. Mr. Lukic. Oh, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have nothing to add, but there is something I need to say about the transcript. Page 3, line 21, [In English] "Vujic being served." I think I was talking about 65 ter documents, those served on us by our learned friends from the OTP. I never mentioned Mr. Vujic at all.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, nor did the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, everybody is disclaimed so far. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a couple of words.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please speak closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're asked to speak closer to the microphone, Mr. Lukic. We're going to have to get you shorter legs or a higher microphone; I'm not sure which.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was much happier in Courtroom III with the long-stalk microphones, I do have to say that. There is an order concerning the dead-lines which we are now discussing, and I wish to say right at the outset for the Defence it's perfectly all right to have these served in electronic form. The Defence has no doubt that this is the very spirit of the order concerning electronic disclosure. However, if we accept the rules of the game, and we may well be in a position tomorrow or sometime in the future to have our own documents submitted as 65 ter documents, having accepted these rules, we know that the other party will be familiar with our own 65 ter documents and will have the right to use them without previously informing us. This is precisely what I wanted to point out. As the trial has evolved so far, at one point in time there was a problem involving the authenticity of a certain document and verification of its authenticity. I may believe the document to be beyond challenge, but if the opposite party wishes to use one of my own 65 ter documents, they needn't even inform me in that case. It seems that I am going too fast. I will just say one very brief thing. We believe that if documents are on the 65 ter list of whichever party is tendering the document, the other party should not be expected to announce that they are going to use the document. If on cross-examination I, for example, decide to challenge the authenticity of the document, well, then, this is pretty much regular procedure. But we do accept such rules because one of these days when we are dealing with our own witnesses and when we have our own 65 ter list, I accept that if the Prosecution does not wish to use the document in their cross-examination, they needn't necessarily inform us previously. What is beyond challenge is that all the documents need to be in electronic form. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Now, Mr. Smith, this was something that your friend, Mr. Moore, set running. Are you wanting to deal with it now, or have him put submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I think I'm happier to deal with it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the main concern of Mr. Moore was that perhaps once the case starts to get a little more complex in terms of the numbers of documents like military documents, if a number of documents were to be used either by the Prosecution or the Defence, then obviously the -- the time -- the time gap to check the authenticity, et cetera, becomes quite reduced per document. So I think that was his concern more not so much about the past, but in relation to the future. So perhaps the Prosecution's position would be at this stage, I agree with Mr. Vasic, I think the cooperation between both parties has been good. I don't think there's been many difficulties as far as disclosure. That perhaps at this stage, until the documentation starts to become an issue in terms of the large numbers, perhaps both for the Prosecution and the Defence, that we revisit it, the 48-hour rule, at some later point once we get into the military witnesses. But at this stage I'd say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're speaking of a 48-hour rule. What rule is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I think that was the rule that Mr. Moore was proposing, that 48 hours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There is a procedural indication from the Chamber of 24 hours. Have we ever reached 48 hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: No. But I believe that's what Mr. Moore was trying to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: He was trying to ease it out 24 hours, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: But perhaps if we could revisit that, if complications do arise in terms of the numbers of documents. As far as Rule 68 is concerned, the Prosecution obviously takes that seriously, and whenever information is discovered we will disclose. And in relation to the agreed facts issue, there was an outstanding issue that the Prosecution wanted to resolve with the Defence and that was namely when the grave at Ovcara was discovered by the, say, international community -- or discovered. I think that point, unfortunately, has been -- well, there's disagreement on that point. And I would say now that the -- we would be in a position, as Mr. Vasic has said, to file a document on the agreed facts that we have reached and we will do that this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It was my understanding from what Mr. Moore put that there had been some matters tentatively orally agreed, and this seems to have been indicated by Mr. Vasic as well. But Mr. Moore thought there was scope for one or two further matters, and if they could be discussed as a matter of some priority, then it would seem that agreement could be reached formally about a further number of facts, and they could be the subject of formal agreement. Could I ask that that be pursued now between counsel with a view to having those facts agreed and that agreement recorded in the record, as has been done with the earlier agreed facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will pursue that vigorously this week, and we understand that it needs to be resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Don't forget Mr. Borovic's words this morning; not too much vigor. Now, that's for the matter of the agreed facts. With respect to disclosure, the submissions have confused together, perhaps, more than one issue. It is clear that there are disclosure obligations on the Prosecution under both Rule 66 and Rule 68. They are different in nature. The first of them is essential and must be disclosed at an early time. That is documentation which is part of the Prosecution case on which they rely. Rule 68 is documentation or other material which may be of relevance to the Defence of which the Prosecution is aware. So that there they can be sure that the Defence has had an opportunity to look at all the material which may be exculpatory in nature as they present their defences. Their disclosure obligations, and a time comes when similar -- not similar, but different disclosure obligations fall upon the Defence, that is as part of their pre-defence brief, which is a time away yet; we haven't reached that time. Quite separately from that, under the e-court regime, to physically allow the electronic court system to cope, there is a time obligation on each party who intends to use a document, either in the course of evidence in chief or in the course of cross-examination, to give to the registry notice of the document to enable it to be readied on the system and to give to the opposing party notice of that document. Now, there are occasions when a party only realises the need to use a document, having heard evidence in chief which raises some new point, or having -- the witness having been cross-examined and something new comes out of the cross-examination, the party calling the witness, whether it be Prosecution as at the moment, or Defence later on, may, in their re-examination want to put a document to the witness about the matter that has emerged in cross-examination. Now, all of that is subject to a procedural direction under the e-court rules. The present direction requires 24 hours prior notice to the other side. In the case obviously of some real surprise, that is not possible, but it has to be real surprise and the Chamber watches to ensure that people aren't failing to comply with the 24-hour requirement. Given what counsel have submitted at the moment, the Chamber is not presently minded to change the present direction that there be at least 24 hours notice. That will remain for the moment. But it's a rule of practical convenience. It's not a matter of greater significance in the trial. And if that proves not long enough because, say, of the volume of material that has to be used during evidence of a witness, then there may be reason to expand that to 48 hours, perhaps. I know that some Chambers order even longer, but for the moment we will continue with 24 hours and watch whether that proves adequate in practice, as it seems to have to date. But it's a matter of courtesy and convenience and not games, and clearly if you can give the other side and the other counsel, that is the other Defence teams and the Prosecution, if it's Defence all of the three Defence teams, if it's Prosecution, just to give them the opportunity of knowing what's coming in time enough to look at it, to see whether there is any question of authenticity which should have been dealt with already, if it's already on a 65 or 66 list, perhaps not so on a 68 list. Then -- and it's also a matter of just allowing reasonably practical working conditions for counsel. If you want to keep counsel up and out of their beds 24 hours a day, you give them notice of 500 documents just 24 hours before. But that's playing silly games, as you would understand. So I hope you will realise there are two separate issues here: One is formal disclosure; the other is the practical running of the trial so that people have an opportunity to identify and look at documents before they're actually used. So that if they need to put something in response to it or question its authenticity, they can. So, with all those words, we stay with 24 hours for the procedural order at the present time, and if that proves impractical, well, then, we will make some other order. And the Prosecution and Defence counsel will look at the formality of agreed facts. Thank you for that. They being the matters to be raised, we might now bring in the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think we have the same problem, the frozen screen, in relation to the transcript. I think the Defence have that problem as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Time stands still.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I have been advised, Your Honour, if you open it through e-court it will work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Somebody can attend to that while I'm attending to something else. We haven't the capacity to do that. Good afternoon, sir. Would you please take the card that is given to you and read aloud the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly swear that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Now Mr. Smith will ask you some questions. Yes, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Could you state your full name, please, and your age?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: My name is Hajdar Dodaj, and I was born on the 21st of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, the witness said "1991."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, you look relatively young, but I don't think you're as young as you've just said.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: 1972, I'm sorry. 1972, I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And unfortunately, Witness, the questions are going to get a little harder as we go along. Witness, you lived in a village in Croatia in your childhood; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: But initially you were born in Kosovo and you are of Albanian ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: But your schooling was primarily in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you reached the age of 19, did you undertake your national service?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: No, not all the way, not until the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when did you start your national service with the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: On the 18th of March, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And where did you do that training?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Petrovac Na Mlavi.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Is that in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And could you tell the Court which unit you trained with and the type of training you particularly undertook?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I was a member of the 2nd Detachment of the 2nd Company of an armoured mechanised unit. That constituted most of my training. I was trained to operate an armoured vehicle, a BVB. It was a type of gun, and I was a gunner. The barracks where I served belonged to an armoured mechanised unit. There were tanks there and transport vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you did your training at Petrovac. And at some point in time did you decide to leave the JNA of your own accord?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes. After three months of military service I fled the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And why did you decide to flee the barracks? I assume it was compulsory that you continue your training there?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: The reason was I didn't believe the -- that this army was the Yugoslav People's Army, as I had been told. And I did not believe that everybody there had equal rights. I soon cottoned on to the fact that this was not the army that people had told me about and that's why I decided to leave. I just didn't want to go on serving in a Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, I would just like to ask you a couple of questions about that. Why did you not believe it was the Yugoslav People's Army anymore? What was different about it when you were there as to what you thought it was meant to be?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Well, you see, the army had already left Slovenia, had withdrawn from Slovenia, and -- I'm not sure how to put this. Essentially the JNA at Petrovac Na Mlavi had already mobilised the reservists. For the reservists to go there. However, they didn't have, or rather some of them were wearing caps, some had the five-pointed stars, some had the Yugoslav flag, and some had cocks on their heads. And then all sorts of things happened. The JNA started withdrawing from some parts of some towns in Croatia, and that's why I decided to flee, because I no longer considered this to be the army that I had taken an oath for to the effect that I would be preserving the integrity of Yugoslavia as country. The moment they had withdrawn from Slovenia, it ceased to be the army that I had taken an oath for.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you say ceased to be the army that you had taken the oath for, had the composition of the ethnic groups of the soldiers in the army, had that changed? Did you hear the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe this is a leading question by my learned friend, especially bearing in mind the witness's previous answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's borderline, Mr. Vasic, because it is asking about one particular aspect, and not suggesting what the answer should be about that aspect. But I realise you are sensitive -- your sensitivity about that one issue; hence, I say it's borderline. You've got away with it this time, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In any event, I think I'll approach it in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, you said you didn't want to serve in a Serb army anymore. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: What I mean is that there were about 15 of us from Croatia there, and as soon as the reservists came to the barracks the number of ethnic Serbs increased, the reservists. And then I believe that I no longer had any reason to be there. You see, we were given political guidance, speeches every morning by the barracks commander who kept telling us that there was an Ustasha army being established in Croatia and that an Ustasha regime was now in power, that was the sort of thing we were being told, and he would also say that the JNA would survive, despite the fact that the Croats now wanted a different army, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said the numbers of the Serbs increased in terms of the reservists that were coming to the barracks. What about other ethnic groups? Were there reservists from other ethnic groups joining up within that three months that you were at the barracks?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said you escaped or left the barracks. Where did you go and what happened to you? Just briefly.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I went from Petrovac to Pozarevac. I and Lorenc Dohanaj walked for about 40 kilometres, then we got on a train and went to Zemun. We reached Zemun sometime at daybreak the next day, and the train official got off at the railway station and turned us in to the civilian police unit there. He said there were two soldiers deserting. At this point in time a number of civilian police officers came in a car. I remember the car; it was a Zastava 101. They came up to me and asked to see my military booklet and my permit to leave the barracks and go into town. I told them that I had neither on me. And then the policeman asked me if I was a deserter fleeing the ranks of the JNA, and I said this was the case. He asked, "Where are you going?" And I said, "I'm going home, I'm going to Zagreb." And then he said, "What, you're going to be joining Tudjman's army there, right?" And then he handcuffed me, they put us in that car, and took us straight to the police station in Zemun, Lorenc and myself. We only spent as many as four hours there in detention, and then the military police came for us and they took us to Topcider. We gave a statement about where we were going and why we were running. We were taken from Topcider to Pozarevac and from Pozarevac back to Petrovac Na Mlavi, and I was punished. I was sentenced to 60 days of military detention, and they told me that there would be an extension of my military service amounting to 21 days. It proved to be a great deal more, eventually.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And I think I -- we missed on the transcript the name of the person that you left with.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: That person's name is Lorenc Dohanaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how much of the -- you said you were sentenced to 60 days of military detention. How much of that did you actually serve?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: 35 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court why you didn't finish the full 60 days? What happened after you served your 35 days?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I didn't for one reason, because we were sent out into the field from my barracks, a group. I think a unit, the 2nd Mechanised Unit was transferred to Bogojevo. We were deployed in an area near Bijelo Brdo, close to Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were you told the reason for your deployment, why you were being sent there?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: No, no, we weren't. They just said we were going out into the field, but they didn't tell us why we were being deployed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how did you get to Bijelo Brdo? Did you bring equipment with you or not?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: We only had light weapons and combat rucksacks with us. We were stationed at Bogojevo. That is where we were issued with ammunition. And then from Bogojevo we were transferred via the Bogojevo bridge to Bijelo Brdo. When we got to Bijelo Brdo, we were there to replace another unit. I don't know where that unit was from. I know that they had tanks, multiple rocket launchers and self-propelled guns and also an infantry transporter vehicle. We were stationed there for two or three weeks. I really don't know exactly how long we were there. The tanks, the armoured vehicles and the rocket launchers were there in order to fire at Dalj, Erdut and Sarvas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how many from your unit left Petrovac Na Mlavi and went to Bijelo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I think that there were about 40 of us, 40 to 60. Actually, I think there were about 40. That's how many of us fitted into the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you got there what was the role of your unit?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Our role was -- actually, those who were picking the targets in the tanks, they were firing at Sarvas and Dalj. We were in the infantry, we were supplying them with ammunition and providing guard duty around that area where we were stationed. The tank crews were deployed in the tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, if you could just slow down a little bit in order that we can record the names on the transcript of the places that the unit was ordered to fire at. You said Dalj, and what were the other places?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Erdut, Sarvas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And for the time -- for the time that you were there, how often were these places being fired at?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: We mostly fired at night or twilight, when it just started to get dark. But there was shooting every night. Far be it that we didn't shoot every night. The multiple rocket launchers were also deployed there, and they would be used frequently in the dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were you told or did you know what was being fired at? I mean you said those villages, but what within those villages were being fired at?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: The officers said that there was a number of Ustashas stationed there and that we had to destroy that. We didn't see anybody there. However, you could see the villages, but we didn't see any people there. We couldn't see if anybody was there, whether there was civilians or not. The important thing that fire was directed at those villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what about return of fire? Was there any return of fire from those villages?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: During the days that I was there, fire was not returned once from the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were you able to see if any damage was caused in these villages, or any casualties?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that. But you could see fire, especially if it was dark, you could see if things were burning. I didn't see any dead bodies, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said you stayed at this location for two or three weeks. When you left, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: After that I was returned to Petrovac Na Mlavi. I was placed in detention once again until a reserve member of staff was brought to the barracks and he was put in detention with us. Then I requested to go and see my captain, and I asked that he release myself and Zlatko from prison, which was what he did. He then returned us to the dormitory where we were, and then about 10 days later, I'm not exactly sure how many days it was, 15 of us soldiers were picked. However, the captain then told me that he would give me another chance to escape, because he said that I had the will to escape. So 15 of us soldiers were picked, buses came to get us, they told us we were going to replenish the units in Smederevo. However, we reached Pozarevac, where we picked up several other soldiers, and then we were transported to Sremska Mitrovica. We formed a unit there, we were issued with tanks, armoured vehicles, ammunition, and we were stationed there for three days. After that we were -- we went to Sid, all the way to Sid with the tanks and the armoured vehicles. We were in Sid for another two days. After two days, we were transferred to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could just stop you there for a moment. When you said that you went to Sremska Mitrovica and you were issued with tanks and armoured vehicles, ammunition, et cetera, about how many tanks were issued to your unit?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I think that we were issued with five or six, and these were 55 and 84-typed tanks and we received the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear how many armoured vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How many armoured vehicles did you receive? If you could speak just a little slower, thank you.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I don't know if it was five or six. We received five or six armoured vehicles, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And for those people that may not understand what a T-55 and a T-84 tank is, can you explain what type of ammunition is fired out of those tanks?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: For example the T-55 is an old model tank and it has 100-millimetre calibre. T-84 is a modern tank, and it uses ammunition of 120-millimetres calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Of the -- thank you. Of the armoured vehicles that were issued to your unit, was there any weapons attached to those vehicles, and if so, what type of weapons?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: A tank has a machine-gun mounted at the top. The machine-gun is called a PAT, P-A-T. Both the models of tanks have machine-guns, and they also have something called a PKT barrel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I'm not talking about the tanks but the armoured vehicles, would they have any weapons attached to them or not? And, if so, what were they?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes. They have a 20-millimetre gun attached to it, as well as a PKT, as well as a Malutka rockets mounted at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did you also receive infantry weapons at Sremska Mitrovica or did you bring them with you?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: We did have light weapons from the barracks. We only got ammunition there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were you told in Sremska Mitrovica what your task was to be?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: They lined us up in Sremska Mitrovica, and an officer, I think he was a lieutenant-colonel, he addressed us and he said, "Soldiers, comrades, you're going to war in the direction of Vukovar. You know that we don't have anything against the Croatian people, but we're going to Vukovar to destroy about 20.000 Ustashas."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what did you think when you heard that?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I knew that this wasn't true. I personally knew that this was not true, that -- as far as there were any Ustashas in Vukovar. I mean, I can't speak about Vukovar, but I knew that there weren't any in Croatia. I knew that there were no Ustashas there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say "Ustashas," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: On the Croatian side. I don't know what to answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you mean Croatian fighters?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes, Croatian fighters. The Yugoslav People's Army would say for any man that they saw that it was an Ustasha, regardless of whether these were police officers, guards members, civilians, regardless of who they actually were. As far as they were concerned, they were Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, before you got to Negoslavci, you said that you stopped at Sid. Why did you stop there and what did you do there?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: We were waiting for orders to continue towards our positions. We were just waiting for the moment when they would tell us that we were supposed to move on. I mean, we rested up a little bit there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, when did you arrive in Negoslavci, approximately, what month?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I think that this was in late August or early September. Early September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did you stop in Negoslavci? Did your unit stop there, or did you proceed through?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: No, we stopped over in Negoslavci. We spent an hour or two there, and as we were passing by Negoslavci there was a Serbian flag flying there and a Yugoslav flag. Serbian flag, not a Yugoslav flag. There were lots of other soldiers who were stationed there. I saw tanks that were situated in Negoslavci. I even think that the JNA had its command there in Negoslavci. That was where they were issuing some instructions from.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And why did you think that the JNA had its command there when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: There was one house where most of the officers were staying, lieutenant-colonels, colonels, majors, captains. Our captain was with us and he went to that house. He was invited for some agreements or something. I don't know what they were talking about. After that we set off for Dubrava. This is a neighbourhood close to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you said there were some other soldiers that you believe were stationed there. What other soldiers are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: They seemed, by the way they looked, as reserve soldiers, they're volunteers also. The White Eagles that were wearing white cross belts. There were people in camouflage uniforms with cockade insignia on their heads. There were people dressed in military clothing. There were Serbs also from that place who were dressed in Serbian army clothes. Some were wearing insignia with Yugoslav flags on it, some had cockade insignia on their hats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And then you said that you went to Dubrava after Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what did you do there?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: We spent one night there, I think, and we were waiting for the order to move to our positions. We rested a little bit and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did you receive that order to move to your positions?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes. They told us to move to our positions, that we were going to cut off the road between Vukovar and Vinkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And apart from that order to cut off the road between those two towns, did you receive any other general orders as to what your role was to be, what your unit's role was to be in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: We just received the order that we were to cut off this road, so that the Ustashas would not be able to escape from Vukovar to Vinkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if you could remind us, how many people were in your unit that went to this location?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Around 70 or 80. Perhaps 75 or 80 people, I can't really give you the exact figure, but I know that there were many more soldiers in Dubrava. I'm only speaking about my own unit that was sent from Sremska Mitrovica to Negoslavci. We actually encountered a large number of soldiers once we got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And was it only your unit that was formed in Sremska Mitrovica that went to this location to cut off the road, or did other people join your unit and undertake that task as well?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Next to us were the reserve forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you say "reserve forces," are you referring to men that have been mobilised into the JNA, or are you talking about some other type of force?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I think that these were people who were mobilised from the ranks of the JNA, but these people were from Serbia, who had come to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And this group that was next to your position, what types of clothing were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Military uniform of olive-drab colour. They wore the same uniform that I wore.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I ask that if we can call for Exhibit 156, please. And, Witness, there is a map that I would like you to pin-point the location in which your unit was placed at this time. And if we can enlarge it about two levels, please. I think that's -- I think one will suffice. Witness, looking at the map -- thank you. At the map in front of you, do you see any villages that were close to the position where you were located?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: You could see Bogdanovac. That's the road towards Vukovar that we cut. And you can see Luzac on the left side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are you able to put a marking, say a circle, in the general area where your unit was positioned?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: We were here, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: We have a slight technical problem. I think we can get back to that later, Your Honour. Witness, we'll look at that map a little later. But is it the case that your unit was placed between those two villages, attempting to cut off the road between Vukovar and Vinkovci?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the unit that was positioned there, was this the unit that was comprised of about six tanks, six APCs and about 70 to 80 men?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how many of them there were, but I know that there were many. They also had armoured vehicles, they had tanks. I don't know the exact number of soldiers, though. We didn't really have too much contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you mentioned a reserve group that was in front of you, in front of your position. Were they closer towards Vukovar or further away?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: They were not in front of us; they were next to us. They were closer to Vukovar than we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court what the size of this group was?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Well, you could say that it was between 60 and 70 men, let's say it was that -- that many. It was hard to say exactly how many of them there were, because they were along to the side, stretched out, so it was very hard to tell how many of them there were exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And these reservists, do you know whether they were of Croat or Serb or any other ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I think that they were all Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived at this position, I think it's about early September, as you've testified, what was going on in Vukovar at that time?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Before we were stationed at that position we received an order to open fire from all available weapons, before we even took up the position, before we cut off the road. And I believe that for about an hour or an hour and a half, we were firing. There were some cornfields in front of us; to the right of us there were houses. You could see the town on the right side and we opened fire. After an hour and a half we ceased firing. We dug in the tanks. We received an order to dig in on the tanks, to dig the trenches. The transporters were also dug in to the ground. The order was to the effect that we should cut off the road so that the Ustashas from Vukovar would not be able to escape towards Vinkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in which direction was the unit firing from all their available weapons?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: We were firing towards the town, towards Vukovar. There was also firing towards Bogdanovci. We were firing in front of us also. These were the directions of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you receive -- or are you aware of any instructions as to what particular places should be fired at?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Was there any other fighting or weaponry being fired in the town other than what your unit was doing when you first arrived?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I didn't understand this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that when you first arrived your unit was firing their weapons. Were there any other units firing at the same time in and around Vukovar; do you know?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Well, there probably were. Since the reservists were there, they were probably firing. It's difficult to tell just by the sound of firing when a tank fires. When a shell is fired, it's very difficult to hear inside one of the vehicles, because we were in one of the vehicles when the firing started against those positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in this position with the unit for? For about how many days?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I think about 24 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And during those 24 days, did you become aware of the positions of any other units in and around the town of Vukovar, any other JNA units?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: There were other units there. For example, in Negoslavci you had guns and tanks and multiple rocket launchers dug in. There were soldiers there, and later on Serb volunteers arrived. They came after us and they were stationed at Dubrava. There was firing from all sides. I am talking about my own unit in which I spent 24 days. There wasn't a single day without firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you say "there wasn't a single day without firing," is that firing from your unit or from other units that you've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Our unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you mentioned that you had tanks in your unit, APCs. What were they doing during that time? Were they firing?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Perhaps if we can talk about the tanks. In those 24 days that you were there, how often were they firing? Just talking about the tanks now.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: You see, there wasn't a single day there without firing, both day-time and night-time firing. Night-time firing, most of all. There was a cornfield right in front of us, and then whenever the wind rose, even if they just heard sounds of children's voices [as interpreted], they would fire from combat vehicles from tanks and from all available weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you say there was firing from the tanks every day, can you give an approximate number of shells that were fired from these five or six tanks - are you able to say - per day?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: If you take into account both day-time and night-time firing, I would say over a hundred shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what about firing from the weapons on the APCs? Were they being fired every day?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And during this time, what was your particular job? During this 24-day period what were you specifically doing?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I was in a trench. Zlatko Zlogledja and I were together in a trench. We had been given an order to watch for the Ustashas because they might come running out of the cornfield in our direction, although I myself was certain that we would not be attacked. I did not use up a single bullet in those 24 days. Not me, not Zlatko Zlogledja. And whenever the other soldiers went looking for ammunitions, Zlatko and I did not go looking at all. Once the captain called us and said, "How come you're not using up any ammunition? Are you firing or what?" And then I answered, "Well, I can't see anybody to fire at. Who am I supposed to be firing at if I can't see a soul."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If I can stop you there, I think my friend has a comment to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. There is something in the transcript. It's page 27 and the line is 25. When the witness was speaking about the shooting and then there were various sounds being referred to, but the transcript says children's voices. I don't think this was said. And if my colleague can raise this with the witness, just to clarify the matter, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, you just -- it appears on the transcript that you mentioned that children's voices could be heard. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: No. No, just the rustling of the corn-stalks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And during this time that the tanks and the APCs were firing, do you know which direction they were firing in?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: The water-tower, the town itself, Bogdanovci. There were houses in front of us. I think that position is known as Luzac. They were firing at those houses too. But for the most part, the barrels were trained on the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you receive any instructions as to how you should distinguish your firing or how you should aim and what you should be shooting at? Any particular instructions from your commander?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are you aware of the gunners and the tanks, and in the APCs, are you aware of whether they received any instructions about where to direct their fire?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Well, for example, the men operating the tanks and the gunners, I talked to those lads, and they were told to train their guns on the town itself. And when they were told to open fire, they were supposed to do so. The same applied to the combat vehicles there. The gunners had a 20-millimetre gun and they fired at the houses. They were not given any particular positions. They weren't told that those were police positions or guards positions. They were just told to fire in that direction, and that was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And is this what you learned from the conversations that you had with them, the gunners?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Whilst this firing was going on during the 24 days that you were in this position, what were those reserve forces doing, that Serb reserve force that you talked about that was closer towards Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: They were firing at Vukovar too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did that reserve force and your unit, did they communicate at all; do you know?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: There were Serb soldiers who went there, talked to them, socialised. I myself didn't go.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And I would now like to talk about whether or not there was any return fire returned on your position that you were located at for those 24 days.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Well, you see, between the 14th and the 16th when the JNA started heavy shelling there were tanks firing from our position, there were mortars firing, and the entire town was virtually ablaze. And then they said that we should expect a rather severe attack, counter-attack by the Ustashas and that we had to be prepared. However, they fired only three or four shells, perhaps 60 millimetre shells, I think, and not more than that. And that was the extent of it. Sometimes they would open small arms fire, but that was minute in comparison to the fire-power that we had. On that day, three civilians surrendered. They surrendered to the army because they did not trust the reservists. They went to the army to ask for help, but it was all the same, really, whether they surrendered to the reservists or to the soldiers. When they surrendered to us, one had a Kalashnikov, an automatic rifle, and they asked them, "Where are you headed?" And they said that there was chaos in town, mayhem, and that you could no longer stay there because of the heavy shelling. It was totally incredible, they said. And they said they fled in the army's direction to save their lives. However, these soldiers tied their hands behind their backs and left them outside for the whole night. There was a planted tree grove next to our position, and they were left there for the night with their hands tied. The next morning I went there to talk to them. I told them, "Don't be afraid, I'm from Bjelovar." I'm sorry. They seemed a little happier, but that didn't last long because they were then taken to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, these three civilians, do you know whether they were -- do you know what ethnicity they were?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: No, I didn't ask. But I imagine they were Croats because later on, once I had escaped, I heard these men had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that might be a good time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Smith. We will adjourn now for the tapes to be rewound and resume at five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, before the break you said that between the 14th and the 16th of September there was heavy shelling by the JNA and the town of Vukovar was ablaze. Was -- during that time period, was the town attacked in any other way?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: It's not that it was attacked, it was being shelled, but that day was the worst shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you said that you were in -- in this position for about 24 days. Why did you leave that position and what did you do?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: On the 24th of September I decided to try and escape with four other soldiers. How should I put it? Lorenc Dohanaj was from somewhere close to Marinci. He couldn't believe that we were destroying the town for no reason at all, just because we had been told that about 20.000 Ustashas were stationed there, Kurds, Romanians, mercenaries, and that's why we decided to try and escape. We escaped at about midday on that day. We met some civilians who gave us a lift and took us to where the guards were stationed. And the guards then took us to the police administration building in Vukovar. We were in a cellar there, they put us in a cellar. They asked us where we were from, who we were, what we were doing there. They checked our addresses, the addresses that we had provided and after that they released us. It was some form of detention, I guess. On that same day members of the MUP captured three soldiers from the same position that we had been at. They were also taken to the police administration building, and they seemed happy to have escaped from the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that they seemed happy that they -- they had escaped from the army, these other three, but a moment ago you said they were captured. Did these other three get captured or did they escape?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: They were captured, actually. They were captured but they were as happy as if they had escaped.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if you could --

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: They were happy to be out of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if we could just go through the four names of the people that escaped with you, if you could mention them slowly, and just say who they were and what ethnicity they were, the four that escaped with you.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Zlatko Zlogledja, he's from around Kostajnica, an ethnic Croat. Lorenc Dohanaj, from around Marinci, I think. That's near Vinkovci. He's an ethnic Albanian. Samir Hrkic from Zavidovici. There's a village nearby called Hrkici. I think he's an ethnic Bosnian, a Muslim. And Srecko Ravlija from Visoko, an ethnic Croat. As for those three that they captured, Petar Kuscevic, I think he's an ethnic Croat from around Split. Rasid Adzibegovic, I don't know where he's from, but he's from somewhere in Bosnia. And I think he, too, is a Bosnian or a Muslim. Marko Kobas from around Brcko or Orasje. I think he's a Croat, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you arrived at the police station, you said you were placed in the cellar. How long were you placed in the cellar for whilst they checked your addresses?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Between three and five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you said that you were released by the police, it seems, some three or five days later. Why were you released and what was discussed with you and the police?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: They wanted to take us to Vinkovci. They knew I was from around there, and those other lads were from their own places, the ones I have mentioned. They wanted at all costs to take us across to Vinkovci because we had fled the JNA. We had deserted. They were looking for ways, but there just was no way to leave Vukovar at the time. And then a police chief told us he was very sorry, but there was no way to leave because Vukovar was besieged and it was only a question of time when Vukovar would fall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: At that stage did you want to leave Vukovar, once you were released?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what about the other three men that were captured? Were they released as well? Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when were they released, relative to when you were?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: The same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that someone from the police station said that there was no way that you could leave Vukovar. Were you offered to do anything, did he offer you to do anything?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: They -- they were thinking about which road was still open so they could get us to Vinkovci, but they didn't ask us about where we wanted to go. They just asked us whether we wanted to go or stay. And we all asked to go. And they seemed certain that they would be able to take us across to Vinkovci, but eventually they weren't able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And who was the police chief that spoke to you, what was his name?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Stipe Pole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, we've had altogether seven names. It's not clear to me at least which are the four that were with the witness and which were the other three. Could that be clarified?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, can you just state again which were the four JNA soldiers that escaped with you. Just their names, please.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Zlatko, Lorenc, Srecko, and Samir. I'm not sure if you want their last names too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I think that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: -- fine for the moment. And the other three were the ones that were captured; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So you explained that the chief of police said that you couldn't get out of Vukovar, so what did you decide to do? What happened next?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I myself asked to join the police administration, the MUP. Zlatko, Lorenc and I. They gave us back the weapons that we had on us when we arrived. We were given police administration uniforms, and we stayed with them in the cellar. We later moved to a different place because of safety reasons, because the police administration building was being shelled on a daily basis as well as the area around it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what about Srecko, what did he do? Did he join as well?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Not long after, Srecko's leg was blown off. A mortar shell landed in the courtyard of the police administration building and his leg was blown to bits. We carried him to the hospital and that was where he stayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you said that you asked to join the police administration. What -- what did you expect that you were going to do? What was your task?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I didn't expect to be given any tasks. They didn't even ask us to go to any positions where there was firing, where would be exposed to firing. Although it didn't make much difference if you were at the front line or right there in the middle of town. The shelling was the same all over. It was for our personal safety that we kept those weapons that we had brought along. They didn't ask us to do anything else. They didn't give us any specific tasks to go somewhere. It was more of our own free will that we accepted this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if they didn't give you any specific task, did they give you any general tasks that you were to do or not?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what did you do from that point forward?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: The police building had been subjected to so much shelling that eight of us from the police moved to a different cellar near the Danube. We stayed there, and at nightfall we would stand guard to make sure none of the passers-by chucked anything into our cellar. Sometimes we watched our town being shelled from across the Danube. You could see guns there, tanks, multiple rocket launchers. We spent most of our time watching that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And why did the -- why did the police give you a uniform?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: They didn't give us a uniform; we asked to be given uniforms. We got rid of the JNA uniform, and they didn't have any civilian clothes to give us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: With your JNA weapon that you had whilst you were at the position outside of Vukovar, what did you do with that? Did you still have that when you joined the police?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you stayed in Vukovar until what date? When did you -- when did you leave Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: When I left the hospital on the 20th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So could you explain a little bit more, just in a little more detail for that, say, two months that you were with the -- with the police what your duties were, just a little more. You have explained that you were guarding the cellar that you were staying at?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Well, the first thing that I wanted after I had escaped from the JNA was to see where those 12 -- 20.000 Ustashas were stationed that they'd told us about. However, once there I noticed the police forces, I noticed civilians carrying some sort of weapons, but - I'm not sure how I should put this - it wasn't an organised army, sufficiently organised to resist the kind of force that was being used to advance on the town. What I really wanted to know, whether there were any Blackshirts in Vukovar, or Ustashas that they told us about in the JNA. But all I saw when I got there was people defending their homes, their neighbourhoods, and members of the police. My personal task, my personal assignment, sometimes we would go to the shops in the area, get canned food or something like that and bring it to civilians. Whenever we opened a shop, all the civilians would come out of their cellars to go to the shop and try to see if they could lay their hands on some food. People were hungry and thirsty and unable to move about because of the shelling. Everybody was afraid of the shelling. It wasn't like dozens of shells were falling every day, more like hundreds. So that was what I saw when I came there. And that's what my assignment was. And we also stood guard where I said, facing the Danube, to see if the army was perhaps about to start crossing the Danube.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if the army -- or did the army cross the Danube whilst you were in that position over that period of time?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what would you have done if, in fact, the army had crossed the Danube? What would -- what did you believe you were expected to do, if anything?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: You mean if they crossed the Danube towards us? We would probably have opened fire at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And for about how long did you stay in the police station?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I can't really say how long we stayed there. A month, less than a month, two or three weeks. I don't know. I stayed until -- well, I really can't say how long I was there. Maybe 20 days or -- I can't really tell you with any certainty how long it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And then about how long did you stay in this other place, this other place that you moved to?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Vukovar fell on the 17th; on the 17th we withdrew. I think that we withdrew to a shelter where there were many, many civilians, a large number of civilians. Some people managed to get out of Vukovar, some stayed behind. Some tried to make a kind of break-through, but they didn't succeed. Lorenc and I, even though later he stepped on this device, which shattered his heel, we returned him to the hospital, so I was in the hospital until the army came.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that you were provided -- or you still had your weapon when you were working with the police or had the police uniform. About how many other men in town had weapons that you saw in the two-month period that you were in town?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I saw police officers and guardsmen when they would come to get the food for the police; that's what I saw. I took off the uniform after 20 or 30 days. I found some civilian clothes. It was dirty. You can't really spend a month in one uniform. Later the entire police administration burned down. Only the walls remained. Everything that was inside burned down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were you aware of other Croats defending the town of Vukovar whilst you were there?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I don't understand the question, I'm sorry. Did I know any other Croats?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were you aware whether there were any other Croats, whether you knew them or not, defending the town of Vukovar whilst you were there?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes, there were. People were defending their own town. I mean, who wouldn't?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And from what you saw, about how many people did you see defending the town, from your experience in that two months?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I can say how many people there were as far as the police administration was concerned. I think there were about a hundred people that I saw. I don't know whether there were more or not. I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you see whether there were any weapons being used other than small -- other than rifles or that type of weapon being used to defend the town?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: The police only had light weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What about tanks and mortars?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: They didn't have tanks. I think at one time the army left tanks behind in a certain part of town and a soldier who was a tank driver actually went to get this tank and he brought it over. It was from a workshop or something. There was something wrong with it. They were trying to make it operational. But then a shell fell somewhere there, so that the mechanics were killed inside, and that's where it stayed. I even think that they did fire one or two shells in that tank that were left. They managed to fire them. They tried to make the tank work. I don't know whether it was short of fuel or something. I know that there was something wrong with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what about mortars? Did you know whether they were being used to defend the town?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I didn't see mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About what date did you arrive at Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I think this was on the 18th. I cannot be 100 per cent sure, but I think it was the 18th. I think that I spent one or two nights, I don't even know myself how many nights.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can we talk about the day that you left Vukovar Hospital. You'd stayed there the night before. Can you tell us what happened the next day, on the 20th?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: On the 20th, well, the day before they told us that those who wanted to go to Zagreb could go to Zagreb. I cannot be quite certain about this, but I think that there were lists of people made who wanted to go to Zagreb, who wanted to go to Belgrade, those who wanted to stay could stay. However, on the 20th we were ordered to leave the hospital, that we had to leave the hospital. At that point in time, women and children and the elderly were separated to one side. We were lined up in front of the hospital in a single file.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Who ordered you to leave the hospital?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: The people who worked at the hospital told us that we had to leave the hospital, that they were ordered that they had to leave the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And where were you when you were told that, what part of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I was in the cellar. I was closer to the exit door of the hospital. I was in the cellar of the hospital. We were the ones who left first, those who were not wounded; and then after that, the wounded were brought out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what happened when you left the hospital, when you left through the exit? What happened next?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: We were lined up there, as I said. Then Major Sljivancanin was standing in front of the hospital who said that -- he introduced himself as Major Sljivancanin, that no one would be harmed, that the Yugoslav People's Army liberated the town, and that as of today, that day, Vukovar was a free town, and he ordered the Belgrade guards to search us. They didn't have anything to confiscate from me. I had a watch, they took the watch. When they searched the people he said, "Let's go, soldiers, we're not going to be here until tomorrow." Buses were waiting outside. They ordered all of us to board the buses. We boarded them one by one. Everybody had to sit down in the buses. I was in the bus before last. And Zlatko Zlogledja was in the bus before last, as well as Petar Kuscevic, as well as Samir Hrkic; he was also in the bus before last. I was sitting with a man called Horvat. He was a police officer in Vukovar. He was born in Vinkovci, by the way. And he himself told me that, "We will never see Zagreb." The buses set off and they went to the Vukovar barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If I can just stop you there for a moment and ask you a couple of questions as to how you left the hospital. You said that Major Sljivancanin introduced himself. Did you ever know -- did you know that person's name before that day?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I think that Dr. Vesna Bosanac was negotiating from the 19th because the army entered the hospital already on the 18th. On the 18th you could no longer enter or leave the hospital. I don't know exactly what time they arrived. Inside in the barracks an officer of the JNA came to the hospital with a camera and he filmed or took photos of the interior of the hospital. Major Sljivancanin was walking along the corridor with Dr. Bosanac inside the hospital. That's when I saw him inside. And then when they photographed everything, then they left. I think later, on the 20th, they were standing outside. There were people from the international community. I remember a gentleman. He was wearing an earring, he was wearing white, his pants were torn. However, they were not allowed any access to the hospital. They were standing next to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If I can just stop you for a minute. When was the first time that you saw Major Sljivancanin, on what day was that?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I think that it was on the 19th. The 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: After you left Vukovar and after you got back to Croatia, did you ever see Major Sljivancanin again in any way?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes, on television. He often appeared on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in what context did he appear on TV? What was the story about?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: When I was in Serbian prison they presented him as a hero who liberated the town, while the Croat side presented him as a criminal who had inflicted damage on Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And you also mentioned that the Belgrade guards searched you as you left the hospital. How do you know they were the Belgrade guards, and what were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: They had multi-coloured bullet-proof vests, also helmets, and jackets. And it was camouflage uniforms. There were wounded inside the hospital who were being treated by the hospital doctors, and they were negotiating with Commander Raseta - I think he was in Zagreb - to stop shelling the Vukovar Hospital. However, later when the army reached the hospital they were standing at the exit to the hospital, the people who had been treated there, and they were showing or pointing out people who had been mistreating them or abusing them in the hospital. However, nobody had been mistreating them. They were guards posted outside of their hospital room doors. No one had mistreated them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that you got on to a bus. About how many other buses were there at the front of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I don't know whether there was six. I know that I was in the bus before the last; there was a bus behind me. There were five or six buses, I can't really remember the exact number. But I know that I was in the bus before last.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A correction, or just an addition to the transcript. On page 44, the witness, after having described - line 4 - the uniforms worn by members of the guards brigade, described and said that they were in the hospital. Sergeant and a -- and two soldiers in the hospital. Those words were not recorded in the transcript. And then after that it says they were wounded inside the hospital, and he actually meant this sergeant and the two regular soldiers who were in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Smith, if you want to follow that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, you said that -- sorry, firstly, where did the buses go?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: To the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what happened at the barracks?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: When we boarded the buses, these were civilian buses, a JNA soldier was standing in front of us, he was armed. The bus driver also had a weapon. They had automatic rifles with collapsible butts. They took us to the barracks, they stopped there. The captain entered the bus that I was in, he read out some names, names of some people, and the people who were inside, and those people went outside, and as a person descended from the bus they were beaten. They were beaten with handles, rifle-butts. They were going around the bus shouting, they were cursing our Ustasha mothers. "You wanted your own state, where is Europe now? Where is Tudjman now?" And things like that. That's what they were saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how many people were called off your bus?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
