utterances.text: I think some 10 names were read out. I cannot be quite sure. I was in a panic, and I was afraid, so in that kind of state you can't really hear everything very well. I know that about six people descended from the bus, five or six people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you said that a captain came on the bus and called out the names. Can you describe the uniform the captain was wearing?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Uniform of the Yugoslav People's Army, olive-drab colour. He was a slim man, and he had a darker complexion. I know the Chetniks who were there wanted to board the bus, but he ordered them to get off the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And about how tall was he, and what colour was his hair, and how old was he? This captain.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: He had black hair. As for how old he was, I don't know. He was about 180 or 1.75 metres tall. He weighed perhaps 90 kilograms, 80 to 90 kilograms. He had a dark complexion. I can't really say how old he was. Perhaps between 35 and 40 years of age.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you said that the people from the bus were being beaten. Who was doing the beating?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: There were people in the barracks courtyard wearing camouflage uniforms. There were also some who were wearing military uniforms. There were people with white bands. There were people from the Territorial Defence of theirs. There were people who wore cockade insignia on their caps. I don't know, there were a lot of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how many soldiers did you see, approximately, at the barracks?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I can say that I saw more than 50. I don't know exactly how many there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did you see how many soldiers were involved in the beating of these men that were taken off the buses?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Four of them would be beating one man. There was a tank parked at the Vukovar Hospital, there were armoured vehicles, military trucks. There were many soldiers in the hospital compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now we are just discussing what was happening at the barracks, and you've referred to there was a tank being parked at the Vukovar Hospital. What vehicles were actually at the barracks when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: There were tanks also in the barracks compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned that some of the soldiers there were from the Territorial Defence, and you also mentioned some soldiers had cockades on their hats, on their caps, and you also mentioned there were soldiers in camouflage uniform and had military uniforms on as well. Can you describe what groups these other soldiers belonged to other than the Territorial Defence, if you know?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: The ones that had the cockades on their caps were Chetniks, then you had the White Eagles who also had the cockades, but they also wore white ribbons or bands, and then you had the reserve officers who were wearing the JNA uniforms, and then you had the regular army. The difference between the reserve and the regular army members was their age. All of them were in the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that you believe there were approximately about 50 soldiers there. About how many of them appeared to be from the regular JNA at the barracks?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I don't know. I really couldn't tell you with 100 per cent certainty. There was probably more than 50 soldiers. I don't know how many members of the JNA there were. I know that we were guarded by a JNA soldier when we were on the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you provide the Court with -- is it possible to provide the Court with a minimum number of the JNA soldiers that you saw there at the minimum?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I really couldn't say. Perhaps there were 10, more than 10, less than 10. I really couldn't give you a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what about the Territorial Defence. Is that the same situation there; it's difficult for you to give a number?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: It's also difficult for me to give a number of soldiers of one kind and of another kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what the atmosphere was like when you were sitting on the bus and these men were being beaten up? What was the atmosphere?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: On our side when we were in the bus, it was terrible to watch, because we all knew that that's what would happen to us, too, when we saw them beating these people. The person next to me took a photograph out of his wife and two children and he said to me, "I will never see them again." I told him, "Well, don't worry, we're going to go home." And then he said, "Well, can't you see what they're doing to these people that are leaving the bus?" As far as they were concerned, they were cheerful that they had arrested and captured so many Ustashas. They were cheerful because they could beat so many people without telling them why they were beating them up. I mean, talking about savages, you can't even imagine how severely they were beating these people once they left the bus. They were kicking them, hitting them with rifle-butts. When a person fell down, they would be kicking them. It was a terrible thing to see. They had pointed their rifles at us in the bus, "We will kill you all. There's nothing that can save you now," and so on. We were not indifferent to that, we were all frightened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How long did your bus stay at the JNA barracks for?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: About an hour or two hours. It seemed to me as if I were there for two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did you have a watch on you at the time?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: No. I'm giving you a rough idea when I say between one and two hours. But it's difficult to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what happened then? What happened after you left JNA barracks? Can you explain how you left and where you went?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: After that the buses drove on to Ovcara. There is a farm there, stables, and a hangar. When we arrived, the soldiers followed us. Some walked ahead of us to welcome us there. And as each of the buses pulled over, they would open the door and order everybody to get off the bus. There was the hangar door, and they formed a gauntlet with 15 people on either side. These people were forced to run the gauntlet. They would beat them, break their arms, and some were even unable to walk. And when the time came for the people from my bus to run the gauntlet, Petar Kuscevic was the first off the bus. A Chetnik hit him with a rifle-butt over the head. He fell down and he said, "Don't hit me, I was captured by the Ustashas, I am a JNA soldier." There was a captain standing near the bus, I think it was the same captain who had previously been reading names from that list. They pulled him back up and they asked him, "Is there another JNA soldier among you," and so he pointed at me, Zlatko and Hrkic as the JNA soldiers and we were then taken to one side. Next to the hangar there were two JNA officers. They were lieutenant-colonels, perhaps, but they called us over and they asked us questions such as where we were from, who we were, what we were doing there. And then the officer said, "How come there's not a single Serb amongst you?" And he motioned with his hand. He said, "Do you see those fields over there? That's where my son fought hand to hand with the Ustashas. We'll see who got away and who was captured. You, you are deserters. You escaped from the JNA." And we said, "No, we did not escape, we were captured." And then we watched those people being beaten. I remember this one man in particular. He called him by his name and said, "Ivan, are you a Croat or a Serb?" This person had a bandage on his arm. He didn't know what to say, so he cracked him over the arm. This was beating, pure and simple. An act of horror, chaos. And until they'd emptied all the buses, there was this soldier or a reservist, he climbed on top of a bulldozer, a yellow bulldozer that was parked next to the hangar, switched on the ignition and left it running. But at this point in time, a JNA officer came in a Puch, P-u-h [as interpreted] vehicle, he had a personal driver who drove him there. He left the vehicle, walked up to the hangar, had a look, he was talking to the soldiers there about something, and he came up to us and he ordered us to get on that -- to get into that vehicle. The four of us got into the vehicle and were taken to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If I could stop you there for a moment. Thank you for that. Can you just tell the Court again who the four people were that got into that vehicle with the JNA officer?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Zlatko Zlogledja, Petar Kuscevic, Samir Hrkic, and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, it's correct that you all fought with the JNA, is that right, in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I don't understand the question, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: All of you, the four of you in -- initially in the JNA unit in Vukovar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Why do you think you were selected to go into that vehicle and not placed in the hangar? Are you able to say?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Well, because Petar Kuscevic told them we had been captured by the Ustashas, something like that, that's how we managed to save our lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if we can just go back to when you first arrived at the hangar. About how many buses actually arrived there, including your own bus, or the bus you were in?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Five or six. I know that I was in the penultimate bus, and I watched the other bus being emptied. It's difficult to say, five or six, I can't say. Between five and six.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said when you left the hospital that there was a JNA soldier as a guard on the bus. What happened to that JNA soldier?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Well, he came to Ovcara with us. Then he left the bus and I have no idea what became of him later on. But he was in front of the hangar too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how long did you stay at the hangar from the time that you arrived on the buses until the time that you left in the vehicle with the JNA officer?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Between one and two hours, thereabouts. I know that it was a sunny day, a beautiful day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you may have said it in your testimony already, but can you tell the Court about how many people were involved in the beatings of the men as they came off the buses?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: There were about 30 people making up the gauntlet, 15 of them on either side. About 30 people altogether. Although there were people milling around the buses too. I remember when we were talking to those lieutenant-colonels and other JNA officers, I know that at one point a Chetnik walked up to us, he said that there was a Serb inside the hangar who was entirely blameless and asked to be released and allowed to leave the hangar. He said he knew this man personally. And this other one told him that he could go ahead and release that person, and eventually they let him go.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know what groups or group these men belonged to, the ones that were beating up the detainees as they came off the bus? You've talked about Chetniks, you've talked about Territorial Defence, you've talked about reserve soldiers, you've talked about regular soldiers. Can you give us an idea as to who these people were?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: When they were calling out names, those people I think were Serbs from Vukovar. But there were reservists there too. Those doing the beating were natives, local people. You could say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say that there were reservists there as well, what were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: JNA uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that there were about 30 people involved in the beatings, but there were also some other people there as well. In total about how many people were present whilst these men were being beaten, including the ones that were doing the beating?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to give you an exact figure. There were people behind the bus, people in front of the bus. It was difficult to say at the time, but there were quite many of them. Quite many, over 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court what the atmosphere was like when you arrived at the front of the hangar and then these men were being beaten? What was the atmosphere like there?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: We were gripped by an enormous fear, and they seemed happy to have an opportunity to beat people. They were happy because they had liberated Vukovar. They were happy -- they were happy; that was it. They were furious with the Ustashas. That's what the atmosphere was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that you were questioned by two JNA lieutenant-colonels, you said perhaps they were lieutenant-colonels. Can you describe what they were wearing and describe their age and their height and their build?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: As tall as I, olive-drab uniform, a military windcheater, olive-drab, hair greying, crew-cut, neat and orderly, clean. Their age, over 40, I would say. That's what I reckon at least. I know that they were important people there, because when this Chetnik came along to ask for that man to be released and they gave him approval, if they were in a position to grant approval in relation to this particular individual, they probably would have been able to have everyone released if they'd wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what about the build of both of them? Were they thin, fat, regular?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Stoutish.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you said that they were about the same height as you are. It's hard to tell how high you are, sitting down, but what's your height?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't know exactly, but they were about 170 centimetres tall, or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You also said that there was a -- actually, I have forgotten what you actually said. You said there was an excavator or a digger or something like that turned on. I haven't got the word right, but there was some vehicle that was turned on. Can you describe what that was?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: We call it an ICB. It has a bucket in front, it's usually called an excavator. There is a mechanic arm at the back for digging trenches. It was yellow, it had tyres, all four tyres equal in size. It has a cabin on top.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did it have anything at the front, any piece of machinery at the front of it?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes. A bucket for shoving earth, for loading earth and gravel, that's what it's used for. I think the capacity is about two cubic metres of pebbles or gravel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did you see that vehicle, I think you referred to it as a yellow bulldozer, did you see that go anywhere?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: No. I didn't. I just saw a soldier jump on it, switch the ignition on, and it was left running.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that you were taken -- I may have interrupted you, but I think you said that you were taken to Negoslavci by this JNA officer; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what happened when you got to Negoslavci, where you went?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: We got to a house in Negoslavci, we were blindfolded on our way out of the vehicle and our hands were tied. They took us to the cellar. There was a bench or a plank where we sat down. I heard that there were other civilians inside who were locked there. There was a police officer from Varazdin who had been wounded. He was lying on a stretcher. JNA soldiers guarded us inside. One was from Cacak. There was another from Karlovac. I don't know about the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how many JNA soldiers were guarding you inside?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: They would come in shifts, three or four men. Sometimes three, sometimes four.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in this house in Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I think I spent two nights there, three, possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you said that you heard that there were other civilians inside who were locked there when you arrived. Did you ever get to see any other people inside that house other than the four of you and the JNA soldiers?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: People came and went, Chetniks did. I remember this particular person from Varazdin. He was being beaten. One of them asked him, "You're from Varazdin, what are you doing here in Vukovar?" And he said he had been sent there or told to go there. This man produced a knife and beat him in the eye with it so much that the handle of the knife broke. If this man is still alive, I don't think he can -- he has probably lost the use of his eye. And the other people were being beaten by the JNA soldiers. They would play some music, dance to it, and kick these people with their boots. They were taken from the cellar before we eventually left. I don't know where they took them to, or what they did to them. As for Negoslavci, we were being interrogated by JNA officers in that cellar, security officers. They were asking questions like, "How come the Ustashas got hold of you, captured you?" And then Petar Kuscevic said that he and Samir Hrkic had been captured, although Samir Hrkic had escaped with me, and that Zlatko and I had deserted. So they stepped up the interrogation in relation to the two of us and there was some rough-and-tumble. We were beaten, after which we were taken to Topcider, the barracks at Topcider. We were there for 14 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If I can just stop you there. You said that this man from Varazdin was being beaten. And you said others were being beaten as well. About how many people in that house did you see with your own eyes being beaten?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I think about 20 civilians. Most of them elderly people, not really young. People aged over 40. I don't think a single person there was under 40 years of age.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you explain to the Court what the severity of the beatings was like? Were they light beatings or were they more severe? Can you give more explanation as to the nature of them?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I'm not sure how to describe that, but imagine a military boot, when you kick somebody, if you toe punt them with the tip of the military boot, that is not a slight blow, it's more like a severe blow, and the pain it causes is quite severe. People were breaking down crying and they would pull them back up to hit them more.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that JNA soldiers were doing the beatings. Do you know which unit they were from?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I don't know which unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know how far this house was from the headquarters that you believed were in Negoslavci when you first arrived?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I don't know. There's a grocery store in Negoslavci, I remember that, a shop. So this house was closer to Vukovar. But I know that there was a shop there. That was during our time at Negoslavci. At around 6.00 or 7.00 a.m., there would be a change of guard. This soldier from Cacak would come, and he would tell us and his fellow soldiers there, "I have news for you, you know what happened at Ovcara, our Chetniks killed about 600 Ustashas there." We were dumb-struck and were shocked at how they could have killed so many people. And then Zlatko said, "Those were probably the people from the bus. They killed them all."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that this soldier from Cacak told his fellow soldiers as to what had happened. What uniform or, if anything, what was this person wearing?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: The JNA uniform. He was a regular soldier. I think he might have joined the army in March, the same time as I, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And why do you think that?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Well, we talked and he asked which barracks we had been in and when we had joined the army. And then he said we were the same generation, all recruited in March. He said something about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the civilians that you saw were beaten, are you able to say what ethnic group they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I think they were Croats, because they were swearing and cursing their Ustasha mother, and that led me to believe that they were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you said after being in this house for a few days you were taken to Topcider. Where is that?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Topcider is in Serbia. It's a large barracks near Zemun, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And who took you there? How did you get there?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: We were taken away in a military paddy wagon. The military police drove us to Topcider in a military paddy wagon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you remind us who were the people with you that were taken to Topcider?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Zlatko Zlogledja, Petar Kuscevic and Samir Hrkic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, you said you were taken to Topcider for about 14 days. Can you very briefly explain what happened there?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: All hell broke lose at Topcider. We were interrogated by soldiers, how many Serbs we killed, how many Serbs we slit the throats of, why did you desert from the JNA, they beat us. They broke all my ribs. On the right-hand side of my body, all my ribs were broken. My spine was damaged, my arm was smashed. It's difficult to describe the severity of the beatings. We would fall down, we would lose consciousness. Zlatko Zlogledja was beaten so badly that I had to carry him to the toilet. He was no longer able to stand his own two feet. We were beaten by regular JNA soldiers most of the time. Sometimes the reservists came in to join the beating.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how many times in that 14-day period were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you provide a statement to any of the people at Topcider in relation to what you did in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes, he was a sergeant, I believe. But you see, this was my second time at Topcider. Because I had escaped from the barracks and then they brought me there, I gave a statement there, and now they realised that I was there for the second time, and that made matters even worse for. They asked us questions about what we had been doing, what our assignment had been in Vukovar, why did you desert, do you think Croatia will ever become an independent country, why did you join Tudjman's army, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I thought the first time that you escaped from -- from the barracks you went to Zemun. Am I incorrect about that, or did you go to Topcider?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: You see, the barracks is near Zemun, the Topcider barracks. And this was the second time I was there. The first time when I had escaped from the barracks at Petrovac, and this time around when I was brought over from Vukovar. But it's in the same area, it's near Zemun, the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did you give a statement on this time, the second occasion that you were at Topcider, or not?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes. To the same sergeant who interrogated me the first time. It was a pure coincidence that I provided the statement to the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the second statement, was that a truthful statement that you gave as to what you did in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: No, it wasn't truthful. I said that I actually was captured, but as a matter of fact, I escaped. I was afraid to speak the truth. I didn't want to risk my life. Somebody could kill me or something. I tried to get out of it in every possible way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And after Topcider, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: After Topcider I was transferred to the Belgrade military investigative prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And do you know what that -- what date that was, approximately?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I don't know. I remember that I marked the New Year's Eve in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how long did you stay at the Belgrade military prison for?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I stayed there for about seven months. Because I was convicted at the Belgrade military investigative prison to a sentence of five years imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what were you convicted of, just briefly?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I was convicted for deserting from the JNA, stealing weapons from the JNA, for armed insurgency, and also for not respecting the constitution of the SFRY. After -- I actually served a year of that five-year sentence, because I was never before that convicted or had any kind of criminal record.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know what date you were released from prison?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Around the 20th of November, 1993. I was released in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So, in fact, you served two years of that prison sentence, approximately?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And once you were released did you go back to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you seek treatment for any of the beatings that you received at Topcider?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I went to the institute for medical research in Zagreb. I spent about three weeks at the hospital. They X-rayed everything. They found that my ribs had been broken. My hand was X-rayed; there are fractures in my hand. They found that I had had a mild concussion, some nerve damage. They didn't really conduct all the tests properly, because subsequently I had a serious operation and I pulled through by a hair. I had blood clots and different things. When I go back, I have to have an operation on my knee. There's increased acidity in the lower extremities, so that I suffer from excess water in that part of my body. And all of this is thanks to the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, if we could just go back. You said you served seven months at the Belgrade military prison. The remainder of your two-year sentence, where was that served?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes. I was transferred to the central prison in Serbia from the investigative prison, I spent some time there. After that, I was transferred to the Valjevo correction centre, and that's where I served the rest of my sentence, and that's where I was released from.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I'm just going to ask you to look at now a couple of documents that will appear on the computer screen. And the first one I would ask that be shown is Exhibit 103, which is the eastern Croatian map. This is not 103, but we can do this one now and then go back to the 103. If we can just enlarge it a couple of sizes, please. Witness, this is Exhibit 156. Do you recognise that map on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Bogdanovci, Vukovar, Luzac, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: With the pen which I believe will work now, can you put a red ring, or whatever colour is in it, around the village of Bogdanovci, and a ring around Luzac?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And approximately could you put the position that your unit was located in for that 24 days that you were with the JNA army? Just the approximate area.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I seek to tender that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit 233.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if I can ask for exhibit number 103, please. And if that could be enlarged one more level from that point, please. Thank you. Perhaps if it can move to the left. And then -- that's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, do you see this map in front of you?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned that when you first went to Croatia with the JNA you went to a place called -- near Osijek called Bijelo Brdo. That location doesn't appear on this particular map, but you also gave testimony that the unit that you were with fired on a few villages. Can you circle the villages that your unit fired on, please, with the pen?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And you have circled Sarvas, Dalj and Erdut. Although Bijelo Brdo doesn't appear on this map, can you put the approximate location where that village is. If you can't, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You are unable to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter was unable to hear whether the witness said yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the Bogojevo bridge should be somewhere around there. I don't know where the bridge is, but it's from the direction of Vojvodina, I think Bijelo Brdo could be somewhere here, approximately, but I can't tell you exactly where it was. More or less, I'm not sure if it's there or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I seek to tender that map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit 234.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if I can ask for Exhibit 170, please. Photograph 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, looking at this photograph in front of you, do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what is it a photograph of?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: This is the entrance to the hospital. This is the wall where we were lined up. I think that this is the emergency service entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you draw a line on the photograph showing where you were lined up with the others?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: In this direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The -- how many people were in the line?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I don't know how many. We were lined up all along the wall practically to the exit. There were a lot of people lined up in a long column.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you draw an arrow in the -- depicting the direction that you left to go towards the buses?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I seek to tender that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit 235.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the last exhibit, 65 ter, 228. And the photo number 22 of 26, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, do you see the photograph on the computer screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that detainees were taken off the buses and placed into the hangar. Do you know which hangar they were placed into?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: The first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you draw a ring around that hangar, please?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And with a cross, can you mark the entrance to the hangar that you saw the detainees taken into?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Mark it with what?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: A cross, an X.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you said that you saw a soldier start a yellow bulldozer. Are you able to say, in relation to that hangar, where that bulldozer was started up?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if you can mark that with an A, please, just next to it, the letter A.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Might be my glasses again, Your Honour, but I assume it's a it's a letter A. Your Honour, that's the questions for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you tender this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I seek to tender that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit 236.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will adjourn now and resume at 10 past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dodaj, good evening. I am Vladimir Domazet, one of the Defence counsel for Mr. Mrksic. I am going to be asking you questions, and I would ask you to make a little pause before you begin answering because we are both using the same language and if we don't make a break, it will be more difficult for the interpreters to interpret everything that we are saying.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Good evening to you as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Dodaj, as a witness you provided statements to different police and judiciary institutions several times.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you recall who you gave the statements to about all the things that you discussed here today?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I gave a statement to the police administration in Bjelovar; in Zagreb, I think that I also provided a statement; in 1998 I provided a statement here in The Hague; in 2004 in Belgrade; and then once again here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to remind you, and you will tell me whether you recollect that and whether that is correct, we will see if there is perhaps a statement that I don't know about or a statement that you do not recall. You mentioned Bjelovar. You provided a statement at the MUP in Bjelovar; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: According to my information, this was in 1994.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: After that you provided a statement to the investigators of The Hague Tribunal. This was sometime in April 1996. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I think that that was so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was that the only statement provided to The Hague investigators until you came here now, on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I think also I provided a statement in 1998 in the Dokmanovic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember that that same year, 1996, you provided a statement to a court in Bjelovar?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I think that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember which case that was?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I think it was a case -- the case against Veljko Kadijevic and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that you gave a statement in Zagreb in 2004.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: No, I didn't say in 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I gave a statement in Belgrade in 2004. I was questioned by investigators from Belgrade in Zagreb. I don't know whether this was one month before. I can't really be sure about the date, but it was in 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, I was going precisely in that order. The statement that you provided to the investigators in Zagreb was before you testified in Belgrade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: According to my information, you testified in Belgrade in October 2004 at the trial itself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What you mentioned in Zagreb as having taken place before that, you said that you gave a statement to investigators. Am I right when I say that this happened to be in the district court in Zagreb itself, and that you were questioned by the investigating judge there?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, it was the investigating judge. But the gentlemen were from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. Do you remember that there was a judge from Belgrade present as well as a prosecutor? Is that correct? In any case, there were a number of people who attended this interrogation of yours or deposition?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Except the statement in Zagreb when people from Belgrade were present, did you provide any other statements in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I don't think that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Very well. I would like to ask some questions about your particulars, which were not covered in the questions put earlier. Based on the information available, you were born in Djakovica. Djakovica is in Kosovo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes, in Novoselle.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Near Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: However, from your early childhood you were -- have been living in Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember the year, because there is some information that this was from 1978. Can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes, from 1978.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you were about six years old then?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes, six years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I assume that at that time your whole family moved to Bjelovar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: My mother, father, brothers and sisters, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You had one sister and four brothers who lived with you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I assume that your father supported you, your parents supported you. What did your father do?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: For a while he worked in the farming business, then he got a job at the road maintenance company. He spent some time working in Switzerland as well. And now he's a farmer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You have your own house where you lived and where you still live?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes, we bought a house in 1978. Although I have my own house now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said that sometime in March 1991 you went to serve your military term of duty in the JNA. Based on the information you provided, I assume that you were recruited in Bjelovar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes, in the defence department in Bjelovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: That's where you were recruited and you passed all the medical examinations and other tests required and then you were sent to serve and the first place that you served was Petrovac Na Mlavi; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And Petrovac Na Mlavi, where you began your military term of duty, you talked about what was happening there a few months later. But when you just arrived, the unit that you were in, am I right if I say that at that time it was a multi-ethnic unit, that it comprised soldiers from various ethnic groups from the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes, you could say that. They were from Croatia, Bosnia, Macedonia. There was nobody from Slovenia though.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know why there were no soldiers from Slovenia? Was it already a question of Slovenia not sending its people there or something else?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: There was one Slovenian in the barracks, so when the JNA withdrew, he was allowed to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. But I understood that in your generation there were no Slovenians?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: That's correct. There were no Slovenians in my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Your commander at the time, which ethnic group did he belong to?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: The section commander was Esad Halilovic, the commander of the 2nd Company was Captain Majtan Mihajl. The barracks commander was First Class Captain Radenko Jovic. I think that that was his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. This captain, Majtan, if I recall the last name properly, I think you discussed him in your statements you. Said that he was Hungarian. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Well, I understood by his last name that he was Hungarian. I think that's his -- that was his ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did he ever say anything in conversations with you about that or did you just get the impression that he was an ethnic Hungarian?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Well, that's what the soldiers who were from Vojvodina told me. There were some Hungarian, ethnic Hungarian soldiers who said that this last name was Hungarian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And this Esad you mentioned, where was he from?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I think that he was from Novi Pazar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I don't know his ethnicity, but I think he was a Muslim by religion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. When you spoke about what I will call your first attempt to leave the JNA, you gave us an account of how you reached Zemun by train and then a train official turned you into the police. Were you travelling in uniform or in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: In uniform, the JNA uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you not have your civilian clothes with you?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes, back at the barracks I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Just for the benefit of the Chamber, they may not be that familiar with the subject, at the time soldiers serving their military term with the JNA were entitled to have their own civilian clothes with them and to wear these when on leave or when away from the barracks?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, but not in their own lockers. There was a different room where the civilian clothes were kept. And when, for example, you would leave the barracks to go to town, you would sign for a set of civilian clothes. At the time when I fled the barracks, I was not able to retrieve my civilian clothes, so I escaped in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you carry any weapons or anything?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I was without weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: This train official, how did he learn who you were? Did he tell you something, did you ask him something, or did he just have suspicions? Did you give him a reason to believe that you were deserters?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes. When we got off the train at Pozarevac, we first wanted to buy a ticket for Belgrade. We didn't realise that the train was only going as far as Zemun. It was on the train when we started talking to the train official that we found out if the train was going as far as Zemun and he said, "Well, are you going to Belgrade or to Zemun?" And then we said, "We're going to Zemun," and that probably betrayed us, and he started having suspicions about who we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you were first taken to Topcider and then to Petrovac Na Mlavi?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: First Pozarevac and then Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You -- disciplinary steps were taken against you. You didn't face a court-martial or anything?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: No. This is military remand, because that was after 60 days. Anything over 60 days you are summoned before a military court.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the interpretation. We must slow down for the transcript. So no charges were pressed against you or your friend. You were just punished and that was that, the 60 days?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I assume it was then that you were sent to serve your punishment?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes. They had a remand facility inside the barracks, and we were detained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: It was the same barracks where you served your military term?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said that you left after 35 days. Was it because --

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I didn't say after 35 days. It was a total of 35 days that I served.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So the total before and after. What about before you left?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Perhaps 28 days, just under a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: My understanding was you were released from prison in order to go and take up this new mission that you described?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes, we went towards Bijelo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Bijelo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What about the other soldier? Did he leave with you in the same way?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I suppose -- or, rather, maybe you can tell me, did the whole unit go or just part of the unit?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: A busload of soldiers. About 40 people from the 2nd Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Not the entire unit, just 40 people, right?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes. A handful of soldiers from the 2nd Company remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You told us today that upon your return you -- you continued to serve the punishment that you had received, right?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You probably remember the day you left for that position in Vojvodina, or across the Danube somewhere, right?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: It was in late July, I know it was very hot. We were wearing shirts. Late July, early August, give or take a day or two. It might even have been August.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Very well. You spent about two weeks there and then you went back, right?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes, you could say that. Between two and three weeks, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Once you were back you got on with your punishment, the punishment that was imposed, both you and your friend, right?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But you did not serve the entire length that was imposed, right?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What was the reason for this, that your term of punishment was interrupted or cut short?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: A reservist came along who had allegedly killed one of his own while standing guard. He was visibly under the influence the evening that he was brought there. There was a lieutenant on duty that night. The military police searched him, and he had a small knife for opening cans on him. We had a small bed in that cell, and when they brought him to the cell he said that from this evening on he would be using that bed and we would be using the mattresses that were down there on the floor. And I said, "You can't use that bed, that's my bed. I sleep on it." So there was an altercation, and he pulled out this small knife. I banged as hard as I could with my fist against the door, and then the lieutenant came. First the duty soldier came, he unlocked the door, and I said, "You didn't search this man, he has a knife on him." And then the duty officer came and he cracked him over the head with a pistol. And he said, "Didn't I tell you not to touch these lads?" And then I asked him to send us back to the room, because we would not be in the same cell as that man. And then he sent us back to the dormitory.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Aside from this, were there any other conversations or any promises made about what you were to do later on, how you would behave? Was anything said about your future behaviour? Was that one of the reasons that your punishment was cut short?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: You see, I was more a model soldier than a hooligan in the army and the officers took a liking to me. Captain Mihad [as interpreted] called me and said, "Listen now, I'll give you another chance to escape from the army, because I see you have no desire to stay at all." And that was why the captain sent me to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said in one of your statements, but do you think the captain meant this seriously, or was he just pulling your leg, in a way, or did he mean it seriously and that was why he sent you there?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Once I was selected to go, I took that to mean that he had been serious about this. At the time when he said it, I took it more as some sort of a joke.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Once you were on your way to Sremska Mitrovica, only a small part of the unit left, right?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes, about 15 soldiers. But then the bus was filled to capacity at Pozarevac and that's how we drove on to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When giving your statements your accounts did not quite tally on this. You said you were on your way to Sremska Mitrovica, you said there were no stopovers. You mentioned Smederevo -- please just let me complete my question for the transcript. Do you remember exactly how you went there?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: We were lined up and were told that we were on our way to reinforce some units at Smederevo, only we arrived in Pozarevac not Smederevo. And that was where the bus was filled with the remaining soldiers and then the bus drove to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. But for the benefit of the Chamber, can we agree that Pozarevac is actually on the way to Smederevo somewhere along the road. You just needed to drive on from there?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: No, but we were not in Smederevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You say that the unit was reinforced with reservists.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: No, I never said, did I?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Your unit was not reinforced with reservists, was it?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: The unit that were sent to Smederevo, those were all active duty soldiers, and the reservists had been mobilised in the barracks. Unless you mean the reinforcements that may have been carried out in the barracks itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Which barracks are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Petrovac Na Mlavi.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: That's my question. Were there any reservists around in the barracks, because I believe you testified in chief that reservists had been mobilised and sent alongside with you, right, dispatched?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: No, they weren't sent with us to Sremska Mitrovica. They remained the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Fair enough. There was one question that my learned friend asked about the reservists and their ethnicity and you said that most of them were Serbs or all them were Serbs, something along those lines, right? Sir, these reservists, you probably know this, I believe we can agree, were people living in that town or in the immediate vicinity of that town, and that's how they received their wartime assignment and are mobilised. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Petrovac Na Mlavi is a place in Serbia where you served your military term, right?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What about its population? Did the Serbs predominate, or were there other ethnicities around?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I'm not sure if there were other ethnicities, but most of the population were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: We can probably agree the logical conclusion is that the reservists were Serbs based on their wartime assignment because they were Serbs from Petrovac Na Mlavi, right?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Let's move on to your arrival in Sremska Mitrovica and your departure for Vukovar. You spoke about the position of your unit. You also spoke about the fact that aside from you there were regular JNA soldiers but recruited from the reserve forces, right?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's when we got to the positions, when we arrived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Is this a unit that belonged to your own unit or was this a different unit?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: They were a different unit. They weren't part of our unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you spoke about these reservists, were these the same kind of reservists as those at Petrovac Na Mlavi, they were JNA, according to their wartime assignment, they joined their unit and went there to take up positions, right?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So this unit was no TO unit. They were not TO people. The TO people were organised in a different way?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: No, these people were reservists.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Your unit and the other unit, the adjacent unit, who did they belong to? Because I think your unit had first been organised in Sremska Mitrovica. What was the unit's name?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I don't know what its name was, but we were an armoured mechanised unit. I don't know the exact name. We were an armoured mechanised unit, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But you don't know who it belonged to?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Our commander was a captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Your captain, the one you talked about, you said there was a Macedonian person there, but they changed over time, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: No, the Macedonian was in Sremska Mitrovica. He told us that we would be off to war, that our assignment was to destroy 20.000 Ustashas that we had nothing against the Croatian people as such, but were on our way to liberate the town of Vukovar and the people in it. That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: He was your superior at this point in time, right?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes, at Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What about this term "Ustasha," what did you take that to mean? All those who were fighting the JNA or those that the JNA was fighting?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: You mean me?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You and those who were telling you about these Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: They probably meant those people fighting the JNA. That's what I understood that to mean back then. All those fighting the JNA were Ustashas and the Croatian government was an Ustasha government.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: At the time when you were serving your military term you probably knew this because you had arrived from Bjelovar, Croatia, did you know if Croatia had a regular army other than the JNA? Was there another army that existed at the time?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I don't know. I know there was the police. I don't know if they had another army. I know Croatia had its own police force. They were policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I understand. That was the police force, right? That was the only thing that there was. There weren't two distinct police forces in Croatia, were there?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: No. Or at least not that I knew of.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Have you ever heard the term National Guards Corps?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: National Guards Corps, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What was that, what sort of unit?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: The Croatia army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did it exist at this time when you were outside Vukovar and when the fighting was underway in the area?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: They told us about the National Guards Corps, the ZNG, that's what they called them. And they said there was a police presence there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Dodaj, when you say "they told us about this," I suppose it's your superiors who told you about this, that the ZNG were waiting for you?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: They said the Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. But you say yourself a while ago, the National Guards Corps and the police, right?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Let's try to make this clear. The JNA officers made no distinction between the ZNG and the police. They were all Ustashas for them. Paramilitary units, Ustashas, ZNGs, they wanted to create their own country and secede from what was then Yugoslavia. That's the gist of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, I believe you answered the same thing earlier. The term "Ustasha" implied the enemy. This included the ZNG, the Croatian police force, right?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You say that the ZNG, for you, the National Guards Corps, was Croatian's army, right?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did the JNA where you served believed the ZNG to be a paramilitary unit?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't say. For as long as I was in the JNA because, you see, back in the Serbia where I was serving my military term, I wasn't able to listen to any Croatian radio stations. It was no longer compulsory to watch the news in the evening. All that we were told, we were told by the barracks commander, and I said a while ago what the barracks commander had told us, that this was an Ustasha government and that they wanted to break away from Yugoslavia. Let me tell you something. When I escaped and then was subsequently returned to the barracks, I was told to stand up on that stage there, and people were saying, "These deserters, they have deserted from the JNA, they wanted to join Tudjman's army to -- they wanted to join the Ustasha army. Such people were shot during World War II, and they should be shot and beaten with wooden poles."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said they were saying stuff like "these people wanted to join Tudjman's army," you said a while ago yourself that Croatia did not have an army as such and you said that the National Guards Corps was some sort of an army, right?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can we agree that this was not a recognised military unit and was believed to be a paramilitary unit at least as far as the JNA was concerned?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes. The JNA believed them to be paramilitary units. The Croatian side believed them to be Croatia's army. The JNA considered them to be paramilitary units. But what I don't understand is how come they didn't believe Chetniks to be paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I apologise, it's something for the transcript. In one of your answers you were talking about being forced to stand on that stage and the person who was saying -- was saying that during World War II you would have been shot?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes, the barracks commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All right. That's all I wanted to hear. You probably remember this, Yugoslavia was still in existence, right, who was the president of Yugoslavia's presidency at the time?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: The president of the presidency?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't know what Stipe Mesic was at the time, what his role was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: That precisely is my question. Do you remember that back in 1991 Stipe Mesic was president and continued to be president of the Yugoslavia presidency until the end of that year?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. He may have; he may not have. I know who Croatia's president was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember who was the president of the federal government?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I were to jog your memory and tell you that it was Ante Markovic, would you agree?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Perhaps. I think you probably know better. I really don't know. Look, I wasn't really interested in politics back then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But you do know that both these persons that I have mentioned, Mr. Markovic and Mr. Mesic, were Croats, right?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: They are probably Croats, yes. Mesic is today's president of Croatia, I suppose that means he's a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Not necessarily. Even a non-Croat can become president.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes. Based on special merit, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But he is the elected president of Croatia today, right?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes, a legally elected president.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you spoke about the fire-power that your unit had at the time, the tanks and the combat vehicles, I think you provided different figures. First you said four tanks, then you said eight tanks, and today you said five or six. Let me just finish my question, please. Were you only talking about your own unit or the adjacent unit? When you spoke about this, were you speaking about your own unit that came, that was reinforced, and established, or were you talking about a different unit?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I never said eight tanks in any of my statements. About six, perhaps seven. Five or six combat vehicles, but it's difficult to say exactly. It's a ballpark figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember when you set out for Vukovar, did you encounter any obstacle or barricades anywhere along the road that you had to remove?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: There was a forest there with oak trees and there were some obstacles, but there was a tank driving ahead of us removing the obstacles and burning down any barricades. However, we did not come under fire at any point in time. When we entered the forest, we were given orders to fire and we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you did encounter obstacles and barricades, you used tanks and other vehicles to remove these barricades, but you met no resistance on the way except for the fact that you had to remove a number of barricades?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What about any booby-traps or mines anywhere?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: No, none.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said your assignment was to cut off the road between Vukovar and Vinkovci. A road that had been open and used for traffic up until this point in time?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You say you completed that task. You eventually did cut off the road, right?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In what way?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: We arrived in Negoslavci. We first came to Dubrava. It was from Dubrava that we went to those positions. As soon as we approached the road, we opened fire. But there was no strong resistance of any kind. We just came there with our tanks and we dug in right there. That was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Near the road, right?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: We crossed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You crossed the road?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes. By the roadside in front, behind, beside. It wasn't really a straight line.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. But one thing is certain, it was near the road, you set up your positions near the road with your tanks and your combat vehicles, and you effectively closed the road for all practical intents, right?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Is this the position where you remained throughout the 24 days that you spoke about? You never left that particular position throughout this period of time?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you please just allow me to finish my question? I believe it's been recorded properly this time around, but just to avoid any problems in the future. You carried small arms, right, or light weapons? You were not really there as a gunner operating a tank. You were just there providing security for your unit. You said you were with that fellow soldier of yours in the trench, and you watched for anybody coming your way?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: This place where you dug in the tanks, the combat vehicles, and where you stayed for 24 days, you said there were no attacks. You were not attacked throughout this time. You said there was only this one situation that you came under fire. You were targeted by mortars and small arms, right?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes. And that's when the captain was seriously wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know how exactly he was wounded? Did you see or hear about this?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I saw a 60-millimetre shell land, and he was standing up there on the road. It landed right near him and shattered his side. They put him in an APC and took him to Negoslavci, and from Negoslavci by helicopter to the military academy hospital in Belgrade. There was another soldier who was injured by a bullet. A bullet shattered his knee, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And the captain who was injured there, that's the main road we're talking about, the Vukovar-Vinkovci road, I assume, and he was taken to the military academy hospital, and I think you said he eventually died, right?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I think so, but I'm not certain. That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You heard from someone in your unit?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes, from one of my fellow soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I believe my learned friend asked you to mark the positions on the map. In purely visual terms, what were you able to see from there?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Just ahead of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You were dug in there. How far could you actually see?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: For example, we had a very clear view of the water-tower. We had a clear view of the houses right in front of us, as well as the cornfield. The houses were to my right, as it were. That was the kind of view that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: These houses that you have mentioned, how far were these houses from your positions?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: You might say about 300 metres, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was this a populated area, a settlement, that you were looking at, so the houses were the first row, as it were?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: There were large houses, new houses, but they weren't inhabited at the time. We would sometimes nip over to one of the houses to get something from the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Which village did these houses belong to? Were they part of a settlement or a village?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: This was a suburb of Vukovar. I'm not sure if that was a village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said you would sometimes go to these houses, they were abandoned houses, and you would get underwear from the houses?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Because that wasn't recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I don't think it's that important, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. What do you reckon? You say you could see the water-tower from there. So as the crow flies, how far was Vukovar from your position?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I really can't say how far we were from the town itself. It's difficult to say, to judge the distance, but there was a clear view. A tank's range is 30 kilometres, for your information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, but I didn't ask that.

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: I know you didn't. I'm still saying it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But what about your position?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: There was a very clear view of the water-tower from our position.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You spoke about the instructions and orders that were given to the gunners in the tanks. My understanding is you personally were in no position to hear these orders, it was hearsay. You heard later from these soldiers about the orders?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: That was because you were outside the tanks and combat vehicles. You were actually in a trench that was nearby, right?

utterances.speaker: HAJDAR DODAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have just finished one set of questions, and I believe it's about time to call it a day. And we can pick up tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Domazet. It is a convenient time. We resume tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning. So we will adjourn now until then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 7th day of March, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.00 p.m.,
